cards.back: A distributed, heavily cached database that turns names into IP addresses: a hierarchy of name servers plus recursive resolvers that do the legwork and cache answers.
A question and its answer each fit in one packet, so UDP on port 53 avoids a handshake. Large answers and zone transfers use TCP.
Maps a name to an IPv4 or IPv6 address: the answer most lookups want.
An alias to a canonical name, used to point at a CDN or load balancer whose IPs change. It can't sit at the bare domain, so providers offer ALIAS or CNAME flattening.
Stub resolver → recursive resolver → root (servers for .com) → TLD (NS records for the domain) → authoritative server, which returns the A record and a TTL.
How long, in seconds, browsers, OSes and resolvers may cache an answer. It also decides how fast a change spreads.
30 to 60 seconds; 5 minutes is a reasonable default for service endpoints, and 1 hour to 1 day for things that never move like MX and NS.
Lower the TTL to 60 s a day or two before the change so caches already hold short TTLs, then raise it again afterwards.
Failed lookups are cached too, for a time set by the zone's SOA record, so a typo'd record can linger after you fix it.
Many sites announce the same IP address and internet routing delivers each packet to the nearest one. Root servers, public resolvers and CDNs use it to absorb traffic and attacks.
It sees the resolver, not the user, and caching slows changes. So DNS usually picks a region or CDN, and a load balancer spreads load inside it.
A CNAME left pointing at a deleted cloud resource, which someone else can claim (subdomain takeover). Remove records when you delete what they point to.

quiz.q: You move api.shop.com to a new IP. The record had a 1-hour TTL. What happens?
choices: Some users keep hitting the old address for up to an hour or longer
Nobody switches until you restart resolvers
DNS rejects the change for an hour
quiz.why: Caches hold the old answer for the TTL, longer if a client ignores TTLs.

quiz.q: You want to send 5% of traffic to a new region to test it. Which DNS routing policy fits?
quiz.why: Weighted records return answers in proportion to weights, ideal for shifting a small share.

quiz.q: A '60-second' DNS failover took many minutes for some users. Which is the likeliest cause?
choices: Health-check interval plus TTL plus clients caching longer than the TTL
quiz.why: These delays add up, and some runtimes cache DNS far beyond the TTL.

quiz.q: A crawler resolving millions of hostnames is melting its resolver. What helps most?
choices: Cache lookups in process, respecting TTLs, or run a local caching resolver
quiz.why: Caching takes lookups off the hot path and off the shared resolver.

quiz.q: You want www.shop.com served by a CDN whose IPs change often. Which record do you add?
choices: A record with the CDN's current IP
quiz.why: A CNAME aliases your name to the CDN's canonical name, so its IP changes don't affect you.

quiz.q: Your service is healthy but unreachable because nobody can resolve its name. How do you guard against this?
choices: Raise every TTL to a week
Use an anycast DNS provider at scale, and two providers for critical domains
Add more A records at the same provider
quiz.why: A DNS provider outage makes healthy services unreachable; redundancy at the DNS layer avoids that.
